lesson.title: Make a reaction easier

steps.headline: An enzyme speeds a reaction by lowering its energy barrier, and it is not used up.

lead.text: A reaction needs a push to get started. That push is its activation energy.
An enzyme is a protein that lowers this barrier, so the reaction runs faster. The enzyme comes out unchanged and can work again.
Enzymes are proteins, and proteins are sensitive. Think about what a hot oven does to an egg.

reveal.text: At 55°C the rate drops to 3 units per minute. You predicted the fall: too much heat damages the enzyme.

steps.headline: An enzyme works because its shape fits its substrate. Heat can spoil the fit.

lead.text: The substrate is the molecule an enzyme acts on. It binds at the enzyme's active site, which has a matching shape.
Too much heat changes that shape. The enzyme is then denatured and works badly.

steps.headline: Enzyme B's rates at 10, 25, 40 and 55°C are 1, 3, 7 and 11 units per minute. Which temperature gave the highest rate?

workedSteps.text: List each rate against its temperature.
Enzyme B is still rising at 55°C, so its best temperature may be higher still.

steps.headline: Now read Enzyme A: 2, 8, 12 and 3 units per minute at 10, 25, 40 and 55°C.

workedSteps.text: List each rate against its temperature.

lead.text: Each enzyme molecule handles one substrate molecule at a time. Adding substrate raises the rate only while active sites are free.

reveal.text: You found the limit: the amount of enzyme. Adding substrate cannot help once every active site is busy.

lead.text: To test an enzyme fairly, run a matched control: the same mixture and conditions, with no enzyme.

reveal.text: The control makes the comparison fair. The difference between the two samples is the enzyme's effect.

lesson.orientation: Read enzyme data and distinguish catalysis, saturation and fair comparisons.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Two beakers run the same reaction. Beaker A makes 4 units of product each minute.
Beaker B holds a helper molecule and makes 12 units each minute.

intro.promise: By the end you'll say what an enzyme does, read enzyme data, and judge whether an experiment tests the enzyme fairly.
intro.whyItMatters: Every reaction in your body runs at the speed it does because of enzymes.

recap.keyIdea: An enzyme lowers a reaction's activation energy. Its effect depends on its shape and its amount, and a matched control shows what it did.

blocks.text: You found that beaker B ran three times faster, picked the best temperature from data, and measured an enzyme's effect against a matched control.

recap.nextHook: Plants build sugar from air. Where does a leaf get its carbon?

questions.prompt: Name the energy barrier that an enzyme lowers.
hints: The barrier must be crossed for a reaction to proceed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An enzyme provides a reaction pathway with lower activation energy.

questions.onCorrect: Activation energy. A lower barrier means more reactions get over it each second.

misconceptions.feedback: That is not the barrier. Name the energy a reaction needs before it can start.

questions.prompt: Enzyme A's rates at 10, 25, 40 and 55°C are 2, 8, 12 and 3 units per minute. What is the highest rate measured, in units per minute?
hints: Pick the largest of the four.
Use the plotted value, not a guess about other temperatures.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The largest of 2, 8, 12 and 3 is 12 units per minute, at 40°C.

questions.onCorrect: 12 units per minute, at 40°C. This is the best of the temperatures that were tested.

misconceptions.feedback: 40 is the temperature. The question asks for the rate.
That is the lowest rate, at the highest temperature.

questions.prompt: Once many active sites are occupied, which substance limits the maximum rate in this example?
hints: Ask which component supplies the active sites.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The fixed amount of enzyme limits how many substrate molecules can be processed at once.

questions.onCorrect: The enzyme. With every active site busy, extra substrate can't be processed any faster.

misconceptions.feedback: There is plenty of substrate. What is short is the thing that processes it.

questions.prompt: After 3 minutes, the matched enzyme sample has 27 product units and the control has 9. What is the difference?
hints: Read both amounts at three minutes.
Subtract the control from the enzyme sample.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 27 − 9 = 18 extra product units in this comparison.

questions.onCorrect: 18 extra units. A matched control lets you credit that difference to the enzyme.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two samples. A comparison subtracts.
That's the enzyme sample alone. Compare it with the control.

questions.prompt: A high-temperature treatment lowers one enzyme's activity. What is a plausible explanation?
hints: A protein's shape matters to its function.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: High temperature can denature an enzyme and disrupt binding or catalysis.

choices.label: Every enzyme works best at that temperature

questions.onCorrect: Its shape changed. A denatured active site no longer fits the substrate.

misconceptions.feedback: The activity fell, so this temperature is not the best one for this enzyme.
Past a point heat damages enzymes. Here the activity went down.

questions.prompt: Which experiment best tests an enzyme's effect?
hints: Separate the tested factor from other possible causes.

acceptedIdeas: Compare matched replicated samples that differ only in enzyme addition
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Holding other conditions constant isolates enzyme addition, while replication estimates variability.

choices.label: Change enzyme, temperature and pH together
Compare different organisms at unrelated times
Compare matched replicated samples that differ only in enzyme addition

questions.onCorrect: Change one thing and keep the rest matched, with repeats. Any difference then points to the enzyme.

misconceptions.feedback: With three changes at once, you can't tell which one caused the difference.
Different organisms and times add many other differences.

questions.prompt: An enzyme sample makes 9 units of product per minute and its control makes 3 per minute. After 5 minutes, how many more units has the enzyme sample made?
hints: Find how much faster the enzyme sample goes each minute.
Multiply that difference by the number of minutes.
Subtract the rates first, then use 5 minutes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The rates differ by 9 − 3 = 6 per minute. Over 5 minutes: 6 × 5 = 30 more units.

questions.onCorrect: 30 more units. The rates differ by a steady amount, so the gap grows with time.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the enzyme sample's whole output. Compare it with the control's.
That's the gap after one minute. Run it for five.

questions.prompt: How many times faster is beaker B?
hints: Divide the faster rate by the slower one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 12 ÷ 4 = 3, so beaker B is three times as fast.

questions.onCorrect: 3 times. The helper changes how fast the reaction runs, and enzymes do exactly that.

misconceptions.feedback: That's how much more B makes each minute. 'Times faster' compares by dividing.
That adds the two rates. Compare them by dividing.

questions.prompt: Enzyme A speeds up as it is warmed from 10°C to 40°C. Predict what happens to its rate at 55°C: does it rise, fall or stay the same?
hints: Think about what too much heat does to a protein.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At 55°C the rate falls because heat changes the enzyme's shape.

questions.onCorrect: It falls. Warming helps up to a point, then heat damages the enzyme.

misconceptions.feedback: Warmth speeds particles up, but there is a limit. Past it, the enzyme itself is affected.
The rate keeps changing with temperature. Predict which way.

questions.prompt: Name the part of an enzyme where the substrate binds.
hints: It is the part whose shape fits the substrate.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The substrate binds at the enzyme's active site.

questions.onCorrect: The active site. Its shape fits the substrate, and heat that changes the shape stops the fit.

misconceptions.feedback: The substrate is the molecule that binds. Name the place on the enzyme where it binds.

questions.prompt: Why can't we say that 40°C is the best temperature for every enzyme?

acceptedIdeas: Each enzyme has its own shape, so its best range can differ
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The best temperature depends on the enzyme, and the data only cover the temperatures that were measured.

choices.label: Every enzyme works best at the same temperature
Each enzyme has its own shape, so its best range can differ

questions.onCorrect: Each enzyme has its own shape, so its best range differs. Data show only the temperatures tested.

misconceptions.feedback: The two enzymes on the screen do not peak together.
Temperature changes rate in all of these data sets.
